Treasury Financing Operations

March Certificate and Bond Maturities

On February 18, 1948, the Secretary of the Treasury announced the plans for refunding the $4,481 million of certificates of indebtedness and Treasury bonds maturing and called for payment in March. These securities consisted of a one-year 7/8 percent certificate of indebtedness maturing March 1 in the amount of $2,142 million, the 2 percent bonds of 1948-50 (dated March 15, 1941), outstanding in the amount of $1,115 million, and the 2-3/4 percent bonds of 1948-51, outstanding in the amount of $1,223 million. The bond issues previously had been called for redemption on March 15.

In exchange for these three issues, there was offered an issue of one-year certificates of indebtedness, dated March 1, 1948, and bearing interest from that date at the rate of 1-1/3 per cent per annum, payable with the principal at maturity on March 1, 1949. In respect to the maturing certificates, exchanges were made par for par, and in respect to the called bonds, exchanges were made at par with an adjustment of interest as of March 15, 1948. The certificates were issued in bearer form only in denominations of $1,000, $5,000, $10,000, $100,000, and $1,000,000.

Reports to the Treasury on the ownership of Government securities indicate that on January 31, 1948, about 56 percent of the $2,142 million of the maturing certificates, about 68 percent of the $1,115 million of the 2 percent bonds of 1948-50 (dated March 15, 1941), and about 80 percent of the $1,223 million of the 2-3/4 percent bonds of 1948-51 were owned by reporting commercial banks

and Federal Reserve Banke. In the aggregate, about 66 percent of the three issues were so owned. The ownership figures for January 31 are the latest which are available for holdings of commercial banks.

Subscription books were opened on February 18 and were closed at the close of business on February 20. Federal Reserve Bank holdings of the maturing and called securities, which totaled $460.3 million, were redeemed in full for cash. For the three issues, exchanges totaled $3,553 million, leaving $467 million to be paid in cash to holders other than Federal Reserve Banks. Certificates of indebtedness subscribed for in exchange for the new certificates amounted to $1,637 million, leaving $454 million to be paid in cash. Exchange subscriptions of the 2 percent bonds amounted to $399 million, leaving $216 million to be paid in cash. Exchange subscriptions of the 2-3/4 percent bonds amounted to $967 million, leaving $257 million to be paid in cash.

Treasury Bill Retirement in February

A further and continuous redemption of outstanding Treasury bills was made in February. The four issues maturing during the month totaled $4.4 billion and the amount refunded totaled $4.0 billion. Each new weekly issue was $100 million less than that maturing. The first maturity was for $1.0 billion, the second and third for $1.1 billion each, and the fourth for $1.2 billion. The average rates of discount for the four offerings beginning with that dated February 5, were, respectively, 0.990 percent, 0.994 percent, 0.996 percent, and 0.997 percent.

Beginning January 1952, these columns will not add to the total income and profit taxes, because each includes part of the old-age insurance taxes.
